The story is exceptionally well-crafted and unified. Every element—from the opening motif of the three white dinner jackets and the morphine, to the secondary characters, to the subplot with Eli—serves the central narrative of a fourteen-year-old girl navigating her father's impending death while simultaneously experiencing her own coming-of-age. Early details, such as the narrator feeling that her father's world is a "country where I possessed a passport but no fluency," are logically developed throughout the middle as she finds comfort and community among the men on the cruise, and are movingly resolved at the very end when she literally holds their passports while her father sleeps. The juxtaposition of first love (the first kiss with Eli) and last moments (the final slow dance with her father) weaves together seamlessly to create a deeply resonant and harmonious whole.
